definition: A short, old, or dictionary-word username that is rare and valuable. Usually means created before the Mojang-to-Microsoft migration, or a real English word / very short handle collectors want.
A lesser OG: a root word with a single prefix or suffix (e.g. "Games", "Replay"), or a 4-5 letter name that spells nothing coherent. In between OG and normal.
A username made of exactly three letters, e.g. "abc". More valuable than a 3C because it has no numbers or symbols.
A username made of exactly three characters, which may mix letters, numbers or symbols, e.g. "a1b". Slightly less desirable than a pure 3L.

The Microsoft account type every modern Minecraft account runs on. Two kinds: MSA-Made (created natively as a Microsoft account, cannot be demigrated, safest) and MSA-Migrated (old Mojang account migrated over, can be demigrated and pulled via support).

Not a standard acronym in the scene. In threads it is usually written loosely alongside MSA to refer to a Microsoft account. If you found it in a specific listing, treat it as the same Microsoft-account family as MSA.
You only receive a login token or session, not the password or email. You cannot change the credentials, so whoever holds the email can recover it later. Cheap, often shared or hacked alts.
The account and its email come with the purchase, so you can change the password, email and security info and actually keep it. The opposite of NFA, and more expensive.
In trading threads: a full-access account that was migrated from Mojang to Microsoft (and so can potentially be demigrated). Elsewhere it can also stand for Multi-Factor Authentication.
Partial access: you can log in and may change some things, but not everything. A middle ground between NFA and full access.
An older Mojang account that has not yet been forced onto Microsoft, sold with full access. Rare now that migration is mandatory.
The person who originally created the account. "Bought from the OGO" means bought directly from the creator, which is considered a clean owner history. A "fake OGO" is a common scam.
A major Minecraft OG-account marketplace forum. Also used to refer to the community/site itself.

The information an account was created with, or anything needed to verify ownership to Mojang support: creation date/location, IP, TID, original email, payment method, etc. "All OGI" means everything is included.
The first email address used to create or control the account. Buyers care because control of that email affects recovery and handover quality.
The account's creation or purchase transaction identifier. Part of the OGI used to prove ownership or unlock an account.

An account stolen by grabbing a victim's login session token (often through malware, rats or token loggers) rather than getting the password. Beamed accounts are insecure and can be recovered by the victim.

Having a Microsoft-migrated Minecraft account moved back to a Mojang-style state through support. Because it opens a recovery path, migrated accounts can be pulled; MSA-Made accounts cannot be demigrated.
The highest bid received so far on a listing, e.g. "C/O: $35". Lets buyers know where the price currently stands.
A fixed price at which the buyer can instantly purchase the account, with no bidding or negotiation, e.g. "BIN: $300".
Either the instant-purchase price (buyout, same idea as BIN) or "best offer" depending on the seller. Also written as BO.
Signals the seller will consider offers near their asking price instead of a fixed price.
A trusted third party who holds the account and/or payment during a deal so neither side can scam the other. Using a verified MM is standard practice. Beware of scammers impersonating known MMs.
A username made of exactly four letters, e.g. "abcd". A tier below a 3L: still clean and desirable, but more common and cheaper.
A username of exactly four characters that can mix letters, numbers or symbols. Below a 4L in value because it is not pure letters.
A username or account name in general. A short handle is a brief, desirable name. IGN (in-game name) is used the same way.
A username becoming claimable again after it is released. A changed name is held for a while before it frees up, and snipers watch for drops to grab OG names.
Claiming a username the instant it becomes available, usually with an automated sniper. Used to grab OG names the moment they drop.
The account's 30-day username cooldown is up, so the name can be changed right now. A selling point, because the buyer can rename it immediately.
A secondary or throwaway account kept apart from a main. Often cheap NFA accounts bought in bulk for extra logins or ban evasion.
A non-premium account, or one logged into without official Mojang or Microsoft authentication. Not genuinely owned, so it can be lost at any time. Lowest tier.
The account carries no bans on the major servers such as Hypixel. A real selling point, since a Hypixel or HWID ban drops value sharply.
An account with no bans, no scam flags and a clear owner history. The opposite of a risky or pull-prone account, and worth more.
A cosmetic cape that raises an account's value. Rare ones like the MineCon capes, the Migrator cape or the OptiFine cape are collector draws and can matter more than the name.
You also receive the login to the account's email, not just the account itself. Stronger than plain full access because it secures the recovery path.
A user's trust score on a marketplace, built from vouches and completed deals. High rep is safer to deal with; low or no rep means caution.
A public confirmation that a user is trustworthy or that a deal went through cleanly. Vouches build reputation, and fake vouch rings are a known scam.
Someone who takes payment or an account and does not hold up their end. Avoided by using a trusted middleman and checking reputation first.
A public list marking a user as a confirmed scammer. Being blacklisted (BL) on a major forum effectively ends someone's ability to deal there.
A warning tag on a user you should not trade with at all, usually a confirmed or strongly suspected scammer.
A warning tag on a user who is not fully blacklisted but has unresolved disputes or red flags. Deal only through a middleman, if at all.
Evidence backing a claim: screenshots of ownership, the original information, or a record of a completed deal. "Proof or no deal" is standard.
A second login step on the account or its email. Whether 2FA is present, removable or handed over matters, because it controls who can really keep the account.
Tricking a support agent or a person into handing over access or resetting an account, rather than breaking in technically. A common way accounts are stolen or recovered.
Credentials stolen through a fake login page or link. A phished account was taken with the real password, so its provenance is dirty and the victim can recover it.
Malware that gives an attacker remote control of a victim's computer, used to grab sessions and credentials. The common source of beamed accounts. Never run files from a stranger.
Regaining control of an account through official support using the original information (OGI). The same path that lets a previous owner pull an account back after a sale.
An account taken back by its original owner or through support after a sale, usually via recovery. The main risk with NFA and dirty-provenance accounts.
Payment in cryptocurrency such as Bitcoin, Litecoin or Ethereum. Common because it is irreversible, which protects sellers from chargebacks but leaves buyers no refund.
Reversing a card or PayPal payment after the fact. A buyer can pay, receive the account, then charge back to reclaim the money. A core reason sellers prefer crypto or a middleman.
